title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: It was getting dark when Prince Andrew and Pierre drove up to the front entrance of the house at Bald Hills. As they approached, Prince Andrew pointed out with a smile a commotion at the back porch. A woman bent with age, a wallet on her back, and a short, long-haired young man in a black robe had dashed back to the gate on seeing the carriage. Two women ran out after them, and all four, glancing fearfully at the carriage, hurried up the steps of the back porch.

"Those are Mary's 'God's folk,'" said Prince Andrew. "They've mistaken us for my father. This is the one matter in which she disobeys him. He orders these pilgrims driven away, but she takes them in."
"But what are 'God's folk'?" asked Pierre.
Prince Andrew had no time to answer. The servants came out to greet them, and he asked where the old prince was and whether he was expected back soon.
The old prince had gone to town and was expected any minute.
Prince Andrew led Pierre to his own rooms — which were always kept in perfect order at his father's house — and went to the nursery.

"Let's go see my sister," he said to Pierre when he returned. "I haven't found her yet — she's hiding now, sitting with her 'God's folk.' It'll serve her right; she'll be embarrassed. But you'll see her 'God's folk.' It's really quite something."
"What are 'God's folk'?" asked Pierre.
"Come, and you'll see for yourself."

Princess Mary was indeed flustered, red patches appearing on her face, when they entered. In her cozy room, with lamps burning before the icon stand, a young man with a long nose and long hair, wearing a monk's cassock, sat on the sofa beside her, behind a samovar. Nearby in an armchair sat a thin, shriveled old woman with a meek expression on her childlike face.
"Andrew, why didn't you warn me?" said the princess, with mild reproach, as she stood before her pilgrims like a hen protecting her chicks.

"Delighted to see you. I'm very glad to see you," she said to Pierre as he kissed her hand. She had known him as a child, and now his friendship with Andrew, his marital troubles, and above all his kind, simple face inclined her warmly toward him. She looked at him with her beautiful, radiant eyes, and seemed to say: "I like you very much, but please don't make fun of my people." After the first greetings they sat down.
"Delighted to see you. I am very glad to see you."
"Ah, and Ivanushka is here too!" said Prince Andrew, glancing with a smile at the young pilgrim.
"Andrew!" said Princess Mary imploringly. "You must know that this is a woman," Prince Andrew said to Pierre.
"Andrew, for God's sake!" Princess Mary repeated.
"You must know that this is a woman."
"For heaven's sake."
It was clear that Prince Andrew's ironic attitude toward the pilgrims and Princess Mary's helpless attempts to shield them were their usual, long-established dynamic on this subject.
"But, my dear friend," said Prince Andrew, "on the contrary, you should be grateful that I'm explaining to Pierre your intimacy with this young man."
"But, my dear, you ought on the contrary to be grateful to me for explaining to Pierre your intimacy with this young man."

"Really?" said Pierre, peering over his spectacles with curiosity and seriousness — for which Princess Mary was especially grateful — at Ivanushka's face. Ivanushka, sensing she was being discussed, looked around at them all with sly eyes.

Princess Mary's embarrassment on behalf of her guests was quite unnecessary. They were not the least bit flustered. The old woman, eyes lowered but casting sideways glances at the newcomers, had turned her cup upside down and placed a nibbled piece of sugar beside it, sitting quietly in her armchair, clearly hoping for another cup of tea. Ivanushka, sipping from her saucer, watched the young men from under her brows with sly, feminine eyes.
"Where have you been? To Kiev?" Prince Andrew asked the old woman.

"I have, dear sir," she answered readily. "At Christmastime I was found worthy to receive the holy sacrament at the shrine of the saint. And now I've come from Kolyazin, sir, where a great and wonderful blessing has been revealed."
"And was Ivanushka with you?"
"I travel alone, kind sir," said Ivanushka, trying to speak in a bass voice. "I only ran into Pelageya at Yukhnovo."
Pelageya interrupted her companion — she obviously wanted to tell what she had seen.
"In Kolyazin, sir, a wonderful blessing has been revealed."
"What is it? Some new relics?" asked Prince Andrew.
"Andrew, please stop," said Princess Mary. "Don't tell him, Pelageya."

"No, why not, my dear? Why shouldn't I? I like him. He's kind, he's one of God's chosen, a benefactor — he once gave me ten rubles, I remember. When I was in Kiev, Holy Fool Cyril says to me — he's one of God's own, walks barefoot summer and winter — he says, 'Why aren't you going to the right place? Go to Kolyazin, where a miracle-working icon of the Holy Mother of God has been revealed.' Hearing those words, I said goodbye to the holy folk and went."
Everyone was silent; only the pilgrim woman went on in measured tones, drawing in her breath.
"So I come, sir, and the people say to me: 'A great blessing has been revealed — holy oil drips from the cheeks of our Blessed Mother, the Holy Virgin...'"
"All right, all right, you can tell us later," said Princess Mary, blushing.
"Let me ask her," said Pierre. "Did you see it yourself?"
"Oh yes, sir, I was found worthy. Such a brightness on the face, like the light of heaven, and from the Blessed Mother's cheek it drops and drops..."
"But my dear woman, that must be a fraud!" said Pierre naively, having listened attentively to the pilgrim.
"Oh sir! What are you saying?" exclaimed the horrified Pelageya, turning to Princess Mary for support.
"They're imposing on the people," Pierre repeated.

"Lord Jesus Christ!" cried the pilgrim, crossing herself. "Oh, don't say that, sir! There was a general who didn't believe — he said, 'The monks are cheating' — and the moment he said it, he went blind. And he dreamed that the Holy Virgin of the Kiev catacombs came to him and said, 'Believe in me and I will make you whole.' So he begged: 'Take me to her, take me to her.' It's the honest truth — I saw it with my own eyes. They brought him, quite blind, straight to her, and he falls down and says, 'Make me whole, and I'll give you what the Tsar gave me.' I saw it myself, sir — the star is set right into the icon. Well, and then what? He got his sight back! It's a sin to talk like that. God will punish you," she said admonishingly, turning to Pierre.
"How did the star get into the icon?" Pierre asked.
"And was the Holy Mother promoted to the rank of general?" said Prince Andrew with a smile.
Pelageya suddenly went very pale and clasped her hands.

"Oh sir, sir, what a sin! And you who have a son!" she began, her pallor flushing to vivid red. "Sir, what have you said? God forgive you! My dear, what does it mean?" she asked, turning to Princess Mary. She stood up and, nearly in tears, began gathering her things into her wallet. She was clearly frightened and ashamed to have accepted hospitality in a house where such things could be said, and at the same time sorry to lose the charity this house provided.
"Now, why did you have to do that?" said Princess Mary. "Why did you come to me?"

"Come, Pelageya, I was joking," said Pierre. "Princess, I give you my word, I didn't mean to offend her. I meant nothing — I was only joking," he said, smiling shyly and trying to make amends. "It was all my fault, and Andrew was only joking."
"Princess, on my word, I did not wish to offend her."
Pelageya hesitated, but Pierre's face showed such sincere penitence, and Prince Andrew looked so gently now at her and now at Pierre, that she was gradually reassured.
